key_insight: Real-hardware benchmarking shows that both standard and qubit-efficient quantum optimization methods become noise-dominated beyond a practical fidelity budget, with performance collapsing around an estimated two-qubit-gate threshold.
engineering_relevance: For quantum hardware and algorithm designers, the result highlights that circuit compilation, encoding choice, and error rates matter as much as the optimizer itself when targeting NP-hard problems on current processors.
method: Benchmarked VQE, CVaR-VQE, standard/multi-angle/warm-start QAOA, plus qubit-efficient PCE and QRAO on IBM Heron r1/r2 hardware.
Used resilience-level-2 mitigation and a common protocol across four NP-hard problems: MDKP, MIS, QAP, and MSP.
Compared hardware outcomes with an independent gate-count fidelity proxy (F_est) and a random-control baseline.
evidence_signal: Across 247 method-instance combinations, the study reports transpiled circuit size, hardware outcomes, and F_est; for MDKP and MIS, noise-dominated behavior begins near F_est≈0.1, while QAP produced no feasible assignment on hardware.
watch_item: The conclusions apply to the tested implementations and hardware stack, so they should not be generalized to all QAOA or qubit-efficient methods without further benchmarking.
paper_title: From Circuits to Hardware: Benchmarking Standard and Qubit-Efficient Quantum Optimization on Real Hardware
